papers.title: Photobiomodulation as a regulator of neuroinflammation: mechanistic insights and therapeutic potential in brain disorders.
papers.abstract: Brain disorders, including neurodegenerative, neuropsychiatric, and cerebrovascular diseases, represent a growing global health challenge contributing to disability and mortality worldwide. Although these conditions differ in etiology and clinical presentation, accumulating evidence identifies neuroinflammation as a shared pathological mechanism. Involving microglial activation, astrocytic reactivity, cytokine dysregulation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and blood-brain barrier disruption, it contributes to synaptic dysfunction, neuronal loss, and disease progression, yet therapeutic strategies targeting these processes remain limited. Photobiomodulation (PBM), the therapeutic application of low-intensity red to near-infrared light, has emerged as a neurotechnology capable of modulating biological pathways relevant to neuroinflammation. Preclinical studies suggest that PBM may influence mitochondrial activity through cytochrome c oxidase-mediated mechanisms, enhancing cellular metabolism while regulating reactive oxygen species, inflammatory signaling pathways, and tissue homeostasis. Through these effects, PBM may attenuate neuroinflammatory responses, regulate glial activation, and support neuroprotective processes across multiple neurological models. This narrative review examines evidence supporting neuroinflammation as a common denominator across major brain disorders and explores the biological rationale for PBM as a therapeutic strategy. It summarizes the cellular and molecular basis of PBM, its effects on neuroinflammatory pathways, and preclinical and clinical findings across brain disease models. Preclinical findings consistently support a multi-target anti-inflammatory effect, whereas clinical investigation remains at an early stage, with encouraging results in Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis but mainly negative data on primary outcomes in Parkinson's disease and major depressive disorder. papers.title: The Emerging Role of α-Synuclein Strains in Parkinson's Disease: From Molecular Pathology to Clinical Phenotypes.
papers.abstract: Progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons and the formation of α-synuclein aggregates are hallmarks of Parkinson's disease. Biochemical, biophysical, cellular, animal, and clinical studies provide increasing evidence that α-synuclein is a highly "heterogeneous protein" that may exist in nature in different conformational states or "strains." The various strains differ biochemically and biophysically, elicit different seeding activities in cell culture assays, and have distinct pathological and cellular effects. The ability of different α-synuclein strains to seed and propagate themselves through host cells could explain the ability of misfolded α-synuclein to act as a prion-like agent, spread from neuron to neuron, and cause disease. Notably, different α-synuclein strains can have different abilities to propagate in cell culture and animal models of Parkinson's disease. Moreover, specific α-synuclein strains may induce similar motor, cognitive, psychiatric, and autonomic signs and symptoms of human Parkinson's disease. The heterogeneity of α-synuclein strains may, therefore, contribute to the variety of clinical presentations of the disease. However, the clinical associations of specific α-synuclein strains are mostly indirect and based on correlational studies. Thus, α-synuclein strains might serve as useful biomarkers of disease prognosis and stratification, although the evidence for their role in Parkinson's disease is still limited. At the same time, there are significant methodological limitations to current approaches used for characterizing α-synuclein strains, and much work remains to be done before α-synuclein strains can be reliably used to predict patient outcomes.

papers.title: Peripheral α-Synuclein oligomer accumulation in MAPT p.D750V-associated autosomal-dominant parkinsonism: evidence from in vivo skin biopsies.
papers.abstract: The aggregation of Tau, encoded by the MAPT gene, defines primary tauopathies, including frontotemporal dementia, corticobasal degeneration, and progressive supranuclear palsy, whereas α-Synuclein accumulation characterizes synucleinopathies such as Parkinson's disease (PD). Tau and α-Synuclein may co-localize and cross-seed, but in vivo peripheral evidence in MAPT variant carriers is lacking. We conducted a comparative in vivo study involving MAPT p.D750V carriers (n = 3), sporadic PD patients (n = 6), and healthy controls (n = 6), integrating clinical, imaging, genetic, and skin biopsy analyses. Proximity ligation assay (PLA) quantified α-Synuclein oligomers in synaptophysin-positive autonomic fibers. Immunofluorescence measured total Tau, phosphorylated Tau, and α-tubulin. MAPT variant carriers exhibited significantly elevated peripheral α-Synuclein oligomers compared with controls (P = 0.012), with levels comparable to sporadic PD. Total Tau and phosphorylated Tau normalized to PGP 9.5-positive fibers were lower in carriers, though differences did not reach statistical significance. Tubulin area, fiber density, and Tau/p-Tau co-localization were similar across groups. Exploratory analyses suggested inverse associations between PLA score and Tau measures in MAPT variant carriers. This study identifies a novel MAPT variant associated with autosomal-dominant, levodopa-responsive parkinsonism and, to our knowledge, provides the first preliminary in vivo evidence of α-Synuclein oligomers in peripheral skin biopsies of MAPT variant carriers. Elevated peripheral α-Synuclein suggests a shared pathogenic pathway linking Tau dysfunction and synucleinopathy, although these findings should be considered proof-of-concept. papers.title: Decoding Parkinson's disease: a systematic review of qEEG biomarkers across clinical domains.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVE: This systematic review synthesized evidence on quantitative EEG (qEEG) correlates of Parkinson's disease (PD) across five domains: cognition, motor function, pharmacological interventions, neuromodulation, and sleep/non-motor features, evaluating qEEG's potential as a biomarker across these clinical domains. METHODS: Following PRISMA, we searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus for studies published from 1991 to 2025. We included studies with ≥10 idiopathic PD patients, resting-state qEEG, and empirical data. Methodological quality was assessed using JBI checklists and AMSTAR. RESULTS: We included 89 studies. Spectral slowing - reduced posterior dominant frequency and increased theta power - was the most consistent correlate of cognitive impairment. Connectivity measures (PLV, graph metrics) showed stronger associations with motor dysfunction, gait impairment, and freezing than spectral power alone. qEEG changed with dopaminergic drugs (increased alpha/beta) and neuromodulation (DBS, tDCS, rTMS, neurofeedback). Sleep studies revealed spindle density reductions linked to dementia risk. CONCLUSIONS: qEEG is a promising biomarker for PD, with distinct electrophysiological correlates across cognitive, motor, pharmacological, and neuromodulatory domains. However, methodological standardization is needed before clinical use. SIGNIFICANCE: With standardized protocols and multicenter validation, qEEG could aid diagnosis, progression tracking, and personalized therapy in PD.

papers.title: The "Invisible Killer" of Neurodegeneration: Mitochondrial Dysfunction in Neurodegenerative Disorders, Mechanisms, Emerging Pathways and Therapeutic Strategies.
papers.abstract: Neurodegenerative diseases such as Parkinson's disease (PD), Alzheimer's disease (AD), Huntington's disease (HD), multiple sclerosis (MS), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) place substantial burden on global public health. Mounting evidence identifies mitochondrial dysfunction as a central contributor to neuronal damage and progressive brain functional decline. As a narrative review, this work aims to dissect mitochondrial‑associated pathological features across these major neurodegenerative disorders, summarize under‑recognized emerging mechanisms, and highlight translational bottlenecks for mitochondrial‑targeted therapies. Mitochondria sustain neuronal survival by mediating oxidative‑phosphorylation‑driven energy production, biomolecule biosynthesis, calcium homeostasis, reactive oxygen species (ROS) metabolism, and apoptotic regulation. In PD, aggregated α‑synuclein (α‑syn) damages respiratory‑chain complex I, perturbs mitochondrial dynamics and blocks PINK1/Parkin‑dependent mitophagy. In AD, amyloid‑β together with hyper‑phosphorylated tau (p-Tau) impairs respiratory complex activity, axonal mitochondrial trafficking and mitophagic clearance. Mutant huntingtin induces multiple mitochondrial lesions in HD, while inflammation‑triggered oxidative stress secondarily compromises mitochondrial function in MS. Pathogenic mutations in ALS disrupt respiratory‑chain assembly, mitochondrial dynamics and mitophagy. Beyond classic mitochondrial defects including respiratory‑chain impairment, dynamic imbalance and defective mitophagy, emerging mechanisms such as mitocytosis, mitochondrial aminoacyl‑tRNA synthetase (mt‑aaRS) dysfunction and mitochondria‑associated membrane (MAM) disruption are discussed. papers.title: Safety and efficacy of cannabinoid-based interventions in Parkinson's disease: A frequentist and bayesian meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
papers.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Idiopathic Parkinson's disease is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder with motor and non-motor symptoms that may remain inadequately controlled by conventional therapies. Cannabinoid-based interventions have emerged as potential symptomatic treatments, but clinical evidence remains limited and heterogeneous. We assessed their efficacy and safety using complementary frequentist and Bayesian meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials. METHODS: This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020. PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central were searched from inception through December 2025. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials comparing cannabinoid-based interventions with placebo in adults with Parkinson's disease. Random-effects models pooled motor and non-motor disease severity, cognition, anxiety, depression, quality of life, and adverse events. Bayesian random-effects models were applied in parallel to characterize posterior treatment effects and uncertainty. RESULTS: Seven randomized controlled trials were included. Frequentist analyses did not identify clear differences between cannabinoid-based interventions and placebo across efficacy outcomes. Cannabinoid-based interventions increased the risk of confusion (risk ratio, 4.44; 95% confidence interval, 1.17-16.87) and dizziness (risk ratio, 2.78; 95% confidence interval, 1.65-4.68). Bayesian analyses showed posterior probabilities of any benefit of 74.0% for UPDRS III and 71.0% for cognition; probabilities of exceeding the prespecified standardized effect threshold of 0.20 were 42.8% and 54.8%, respectively, with substantial uncertainty across outcomes. CONCLUSION: Current randomized evidence is insufficient to establish clinically meaningful benefits of cannabinoid-based interventions in Parkinson's disease and suggests increased risk of some adverse events. Interpretation is limited by few trials and participants, short follow-up, intervention heterogeneity, and imprecise estimates.

papers.title: A longitudinal study of rotenone-induced Parkinsonism in mice.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by the loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra. Environmental toxins such as rotenone are widely used to model PD pathology and evaluate new drugs in PD; however, the long-term consequences of toxin exposure remain poorly understood. Here, we performed a longitudinal mouse study to examine the onset, progression, and long-term outcomes of rotenone-induced PD-like phenotypes. A 21-day regimen of rotenone (2.5 mg/kg/day, intraperitoneal) produced robust Parkinsonism-like phenotypes by week 4, including impaired locomotion, anxiety-like behaviors, and deficits in motor coordination and learning, accompanied by reduced tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression and loss of TH+

papers.title: Gait profile score as a summary index of gait pathology in freezing of gait and levodopa responses in Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Freezing of gait (FoG) is a disabling manifestation of Parkinson's disease (PD). Most gait studies in FoG rely on spatiotemporal parameters or discrete kinematic peaks, which may underestimate multi-joint deviations across the gait cycle. The Gait Profile Score (GPS) and Gait Variable Score (GVS) were introduced as composite indices to provide a more comprehensive and accessible evaluation. This study aimed to use GPS and GVS to detect gait differences between individuals with and without FoG (nFoG) and to assess the modulatory effects of levodopa (L-DOPA) medication. METHODS: Twenty-two individuals with PD (11 FoG) and 18 age-matched healthy controls were recruited. Kinematic data were collected during self-selected walking speed. PD participants were evaluated in both ON and OFF medication. GPS and GVS values were normalized using control data. A Linear Mixed-Effects Models (LMM) with Bonferroni correction was used to assess differences between groups (FoG and nFoG) and medication states (ON and OFF). FINDINGS: A significant group-by-medication interaction was observed for pelvic tilt and rotation, and ankle dorsiflexion, with FoG individuals exhibiting higher values in the OFF state. FoG group exhibited significantly higher GPS and GVS values mainly in the sagittal plane, compared with the nFoG group. L-DOPA medication was associated with reduced pelvic tilt, hip adduction, hip flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion. INTERPRETATION: GPS and GVS offer a concise description of FoG-related gait impairment, capturing distributed multi-joint deviations not evident from spatiotemporal parameters alone. The limited dopaminergic responsiveness of these indices highlights the contribution of non-dopaminergic mechanisms. These indices may serve as rapid, reliable tools for clinical and research applications in gait assessment.

papers.title: Manganese Deposition Encephalopathy Associated With Prolonged Total Parenteral Nutrition: A Case Report.
papers.abstract: Manganese encephalopathy is a rare neurological disorder most commonly associated with chronic occupational exposure or impaired hepatobiliary elimination. We report a case of suspected manganese deposition encephalopathy associated with prolonged total parenteral nutrition in a critically ill patient with severe abdominal disease and cholestatic dysfunction. A 50-year-old man was admitted with severe abdominal pain, vomiting, tachycardia, and jaundice. Computed tomography demonstrated acute pancreatitis with pancreatic necrosis, choledocholithiasis, cholelithiasis, and superior mesenteric artery thrombosis. His clinical course was complicated by abdominal sepsis, anasarca, anemia, spontaneous hematomas, and the need for prolonged intensive care and total parenteral nutrition. On hospital day 41, he developed rigidity and involuntary movements involving the tongue and upper limbs, prompting neurological assessment. Serum manganese was 3.1 µg/L (reference value: 2 µg/L), and brain magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated T1 hyperintensity in the globus pallidus, findings compatible with manganese encephalopathy. Treatment with levodopa/benserazide produced a limited response, with persistent severe parkinsonism and inability to ambulate despite gradual improvement in tetraparesis associated with concurrent critical illness neuropathy. The patient was discharged on hospital day 129. This case highlights the importance of considering manganese toxicity in critically ill patients receiving prolonged parenteral nutrition, particularly in the setting of impaired biliary elimination, and supports early neurological surveillance and monitoring of trace elements.

papers.title: Subcutaneous apomorphine and the nonmotor features of Parkinson's disease.
papers.abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a heterogeneous, progressive neurodegenerative disorder in which nonmotor manifestations (autonomic, sleep-related, neuropsychiatric, and sensory) constitute integral components of the disease continuum, exerting a disproportionate influence on quality of life, long-term disability, and caregiver burden. These features comprise both persistent components intrinsic to neurodegeneration and state-dependent fluctuations mechanistically linked to the oscillating dopaminergic tone imposed by pulsatile oral therapy. Apomorphine occupies a singular pharmacological position among the PD armamentarium, distinguished by a receptor binding profile, physicochemical properties, and pharmacokinetics that set it apart from other dopamine agonists and from levodopa-based therapies. Nearly four decades of clinical experience have established its efficacy in attenuating motor fluctuations and dyskinesias via continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSAI). Its effects on the nonmotor dimension of PD remain however incompletely characterized, reflecting both limited research investment and methodological constraints inherent to nonmotor outcome assessment and to apomorphine therapy itself. This narrative review and expert opinion examines the pharmacological basis for apomorphine's putative nonmotor efficacy, clinical evidence across individual nonmotor domains and iatrogenic considerations before reassessing apomorphine's therapeutic positioning within the device-aided therapy landscape. Nonmotor features should be regarded as primary determinants of treatment decision-making rather than secondary endpoints. The emerging concept of "fluctuation-dominant" PD provides a framework in which nonmotor fluctuation burden alone may constitute sufficient indication for CSAI, with direct implications for patient selection, timing of initiation, and redefinition of therapeutic goals beyond motor control.

papers.title: Cognitive subtypes of Parkinson's disease patients with cognitive impairment and implications for geriatric nursing interventions: A latent profile analysis.
papers.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To identify cognitive subtypes in Parkinson's disease patients with cognitive impairment (PD-CI) and explore their influencing factors, so as to provide empirical evidence for targeted geriatric nursing interventions. METHODS: This cross-sectional study recruited PD-CI patients using convenience sampling from August 2022 to July 2025. Data were collected using a demographic questionnaire, the Beijing version of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA-BJ), Movement Disorder Society-Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale part III (MDS-UPDRS III), modified Hoehn and Yahr scale (modified HY), and Activities of Daily Living Scale (ADL). Latent profile analysis (LPA) identified cognitive subtypes, and univariate and multivariate logistic regression explored influencing factors. RESULTS: A total of 246 PD-CI patients were included. LPA identified three cognitive profiles: high cognition-isolated memory decline group (class 1, n=161, 65.4 %), moderate cognition-multi-domain impairment group (class 2, n=64, 26.1 %), low cognition-dementia high risk group (class 3, n=21, 8.5 %).Class 1 had the best overall cognition, with isolated memory decline. Class 2 presented multi-domain impairments (abstraction, memory, visuospatial/executive functions) and significantly worse ADL than Class 1. Class 3 showed the most severe overall cognitive decline, particularly in visuospatial/executive functions and attention, with concurrent ADL and motor deterioration. CONCLUSIONS: PD-CI patients show heterogeneous cognitive subtypes with distinct nursing needs. Class 1 requires memory support and safety education; Class 2 needs comprehensive ADL assistance; Class 3 demands proactive integrated management of cognitive, ADL, and motor decline with robust caregiver support. These findings inform personalized geriatric nursing for PD-CI patients.
